claim: It is generally believed that during economic decisions, striatal neurons represent the values associated with different actions.
source: It is generally believed that during economic decisions, striatal neurons represent the values associated with different actions.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing belief in the field, supported by the literature review conducted in the paper.

claim: Weak temporal correlations in neuronal data may result in erroneous identification of action-value representations.
source: First, we show that even weak temporal correlations in the neuronal data may result in an erroneous identification of action-value representations.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulations and analyses presented in the paper showing how temporal correlations lead to false positives.

claim: Experiments and analyses designed to dissociate action-value representation from the representation of other decision variables cannot do so.
source: Second, we show that experiments and analyses designed to dissociate action-value representation from the representation of other decision variables cannot do so.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations showing that policy neurons can be misclassified as action-value neurons.

claim: Applying a permutation solution to previously identified action-value neurons in the basal ganglia fails to detect action-value representations.
source: Applying one solution to previously identified action-value neurons in the basal ganglia we fail to detect action-value representations.
evidence: This is supported by the reanalysis of data from Ito and Doya (2009) using the permutation test.

claim: The claim that striatal neurons encode action-values must await new experiments and analyses.
source: We conclude that the claim that striatal neurons encode action-values must await new experiments and analyses.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the analyses presented in the paper.

claim: The probability of choosing the more rewarding alternative increased over trials in the Q-learning model simulation.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 1A, the model learned: the probability of choosing the more rewarding alternative increased over trials (black line).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A where the black line shows increasing probability of choosing the better action.

claim: 42% of simulated action-value neurons were identified as action-value neurons using standard regression analysis.
source: As expected, a substantial fraction (42%) of the simulated neurons were identified as action-value neurons.
evidence: This is shown in the population analysis in Figure 1E.

claim: Only 2% of simulated action-value neurons had significant regression coefficients with both action-values.
source: Only 2% of the simulated neurons had significant regression coefficients with both action-values.
evidence: This is reported from the population analysis in Figure 1E.

claim: Several prominent studies have reported that 10-40% of striatal neurons represent action-values.
source: Several prominent studies have implemented the methods we described in this section and reported that a substantial fraction (10–40% depending on significance threshold) of striatal neurons represent action-values (Ito and Doya, 2015a; Ito and Doya, 2015b; Samejima et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: The significance threshold (t = 2) was computed assuming that trials are independent in time.
source: The significance threshold (t = 2) was computed assuming that trials are independent in time.
evidence: This is stated as part of the explanation of the temporal correlations confound.

claim: 36% of motor cortex neurons were erroneously classified as representing action-values when regressed on unrelated action-values.
source: In both cases we erroneously classified neurons as representing action-value in a fraction comparable to that reported in the striatum (36 and 23%, respectively).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B for motor cortex neurons.

claim: 23% of auditory cortex neurons were erroneously classified as representing action-values when regressed on unrelated action-values.
source: In both cases we erroneously classified neurons as representing action-value in a fraction comparable to that reported in the striatum (36 and 23%, respectively).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D for auditory cortex neurons from Hershenhoren et al., 2014.

claim: 43% of basal ganglia neurons from Ito and Doya (2009) were erroneously classified as action-value neurons when regressed on unrelated simulated action-values.
source: Again, we erroneously classified a substantial fraction of neurons (43%) as representing action-values, a fraction comparable to that reported in the striatum (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reanalysis of data from Ito and Doya (2009) shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The permutation test correctly identifies 29% of actual action-value neurons as such.
source: Considering the population of simulated action-value neurons of Figure 1, this analysis identified 29% of the action-value neurons of Figure 1 as such (Figure 3B, green)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B for the permutation analysis applied to simulated action-value neurons.

claim: The permutation test classifies only approximately 10% of random-walk neurons as action-value neurons, as predicted by chance.
source: When considering the random-walk neurons (Figure 2), this method classifies only approximately 10% of the random-walk neurons as action-value neurons, as predicted by chance (Figure 3B, yellow).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B demonstrating that the permutation test reduces false positives to chance levels.

claim: The permutation analysis on basal ganglia neurons from Ito and Doya (2009) classified only 3.6% of neurons as representing action-value.
source: Remarkably, this analysis yielded that only 3.6% of the neurons have a significantly higher regression coefficient on an action-value from their session than on other action-values (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C for the permutation analysis applied to basal ganglia recordings.

claim: Operant learning can occur in the absence of any value computation through direct-policy learning.
source: It is well-known that operant learning can occur in the absence of any value computation, for example, as a result of direct-policy learning (Mongillo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to support it.

claim: Several studies have shown that reward-modulated synaptic plasticity can implement direct-policy reinforcement learning.
source: Several studies have shown that reward-modulated synaptic plasticity can implement direct-policy reinforcement learning (Darshan et al., 2014; Fiete et al., 2007; Frémaux et al., 2010; Loewenstein, 2008; Loewenstein, 2010; Loewenstein and Seung, 2006; Neiman and Loewenstein, 2013; Seung, 2003; Urbanczik and Senn, 2009).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: The direct-policy REINFORCE model learned to prefer the action associated with a higher probability of reward, completing four blocks within 228 trials on average.
source: As expected, the model learned to prefer the action associated with a higher probability of reward, completing the four blocks within 228 trials on average (standard deviation 62 trials).
evidence: This is reported from simulations of the REINFORCE model shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 14% of policy neurons were significantly correlated with both estimated action values with opposite signs.
source: Indeed, as expected, 14% of the neurons were significantly correlated with both action values with opposite signs (chance level for each action value is 5%, naïve chance level for both with opposite signs is 0.125%, see Materials and methods), as depicted in Figure 5D,E.
evidence: This is shown in the population analysis in Figure 5D,E for policy neurons.

claim: 38% of policy neurons were significantly correlated with exactly one estimated action-value and would have been classified as action-value neurons.
source: Surprisingly, 38% of policy neurons were significantly correlated with exactly one estimated action-value, and therefore would have been classified as action-value neurons in the standard method of analysis (9.5% chance level).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D,E demonstrating the policy confound.

claim: Including choice as a regressor still results in 36% of policy neurons being erroneously classified as action-value neurons.
source: However, repeating this analysis for the policy neurons of Figure 5, we still erroneously classify 36% of policy neurons as action-value neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A demonstrating that including choice as a predictor does not solve the confound.

claim: 59% of action-value neurons were correctly classified using regression on reward probabilities in a trial-design experiment.
source: Indeed, 59% of the neurons were classified this way as action-value neurons (Figure 4C, 9.5% is chance level).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C for the trial-design experiment analysis.

claim: Only 8.5% of random-walk neurons were erroneously classified as representing action-values in the trial-design experiment, a fraction expected by chance.
source: By contrast, considering random-walk neurons, only 8.5% were erroneously classified as action-value neurons, a fraction expected by chance.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D,E demonstrating that the trial-design approach reduces false positives.

claim: 32% of action-value neurons were identified as such when regressing on both sum and difference of reward probabilities.
source: By contrast, 32% of the action-value neurons were classified as such (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B for the proposed solution addressing both confounds.

claim: Only 0.2% of random-walk neurons were classified as action-value neurons using regression on sum and difference of reward probabilities.
source: Indeed, for a significance threshold of p<0.05 (for each test), only 0.2% of the random-walk neurons and 5% of the policy neurons were classified as action-value neurons.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed solution.

claim: Only 5% of policy neurons were erroneously classified as action-value neurons using regression on sum and difference of reward probabilities.
source: Indeed, for a significance threshold of p<0.05 (for each test), only 0.2% of the random-walk neurons and 5% of the policy neurons were classified as action-value neurons.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F demonstrating that the proposed solution addresses the policy confound.

claim: The regression coefficient between two independent slowly-changing variables is on average larger in absolute value than when the series are devoid of temporal structure.
source: It is well known in statistics that the regression coefficient between two independent slowly-changing variables is on average larger (in absolute value) than this coefficient when the series are devoid of a temporal structure.
evidence: This is stated as established statistical knowledge.

claim: If temporal correlations are overlooked, the probability of a false-positive is underestimated.
source: If these temporal correlations are overlooked, the probability of a false-positive is underestimated (Granger and Newbold, 1974).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to econometrics literature.

claim: Many studies reported action-value representation outside of the striatum, in brain areas including the supplementary motor area and presupplementary eye fields.
source: Furthermore, many studies reported action-value representation outside of the striatum, in brain areas including the supplementary motor area and presupplementary eye fields (Wunderlich et al., 2009), the substantia nigra/ventral tegmental area (Guitart-Masip et al., 2012) and ventromedial prefrontal cortex, insula and thalamus (FitzGerald et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: Previous studies have reported that the firing rates of dorsal-striatal neurons change slowly over time.
source: However, previous studies have reported that the firing rates of dorsal-striatal neurons change slowly over time (Gouvêa et al., 2015; Mello et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: The involvement of the basal ganglia and striatum in operant learning, planning and decision-making is well documented.
source: The involvement of the basal ganglia in general and the striatum in particular in operant learning, planning and decision-making is well documented (Ding and Gold, 2010; McDonald and White, 1993; O'Doherty et al., 2004; Palminteri et al., 2012; Schultz, 2015; Tai et al., 2012; Thorn et al., 2010; Yarom and Cohen, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: All studies claiming direct evidence that neuronal activity in the striatum is specifically modulated by action-value were susceptible to the temporal correlations confound or reported results indistinguishable from policy.
source: We therefore conclude that to the best of our knowledge, all studies that have claimed to provide direct evidence that neuronal activity in the striatum is specifically modulated by action-value were either susceptible to the temporal correlations confound (Funamizu et al., 2015; Ito and Doya, 2009; 2015a; Ito and Doya, 2015b; Kim et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2009; Lau and Glimcher, 2008; Samejima et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2013), or reported results in a manner indistinguishable from policy (Cai et al., 2011; FitzGerald et al., 2012; Funamizu et al., 2015; Guitart-Masip et al., 2012; Her et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012; 2007; Stalnaker et al., 2010; Wunderlich et al., 2009).
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the systematic literature review and reanalysis.

claim: Several studies have reported that striatal activity is more consistent with direct-policy learning than with action-value learning.
source: Several studies have reported that striatal activity is more consistent with direct-policy learning than with action-value learning (FitzGerald et al., 2014; Li and Daw, 2011)
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: One study noted that lesions to the dorsal striatum do not impair action-value learning.
source: and one noted that lesions to the dorsal striatum do not impair action-value learning (Vo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: The prevailing belief that neurons in the striatum represent action-values must await further tests that address the confounds discussed in this paper.
source: Therefore, the prevailing belief that neurons in the striatum represent action-values must await further tests that address the confounds discussed in this paper.
evidence: This is the final conclusion of the paper based on all the analyses presented.

claim: A literature search using key words 'action-value' and 'striatum' returned 43, 21 and 980 results in Web-of-Knowledge, Pubmed and Google Scholar, respectively.
source: The key words 'action-value' and 'striatum' were searched for in Web-of-Knowledge, Pubmed and Google Scholar, returning 43, 21 and 980 results, respectively.
evidence: This describes the methodology of the literature search.

claim: 22 papers were identified that directly related neural activity in the striatum to action-values.
source: We identified 22 papers that directly related neural activity in the striatum to action-values.
evidence: This is the result of the literature search after screening.

claim: The spike count in a trial was drawn from a Poisson distribution, assuming a 1 sec-long trial.
source: The spike count in a trial was drawn from a Poisson distribution, assuming a 1 sec-long trial.
evidence: This describes the simulation method for generating spike counts.

claim: The covariance based plasticity model was tested in the operant learning task and 20% of sessions were terminated without further analysis due to failure to learn.
source: A session was terminated (without further analysis) if the model was not able to choose the better option more than 14 out of 20 consecutive times for at least 200 trials in the same block. This occurred on 20% of the sessions.
evidence: This describes the results of simulating the covariance model.

claim: Motor cortex data was recorded from one female monkey (Macaca fascicularis) at 3 years of age using a 10 × 10 microelectrode array.
source: It was recorded from one female monkey (Macaca fascicularis) at 3 years of age, using a 10 × 10 microelectrode array (Blackrock Microsystems) with 0.4 mm inter-electrode distance.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods for motor cortex recordings.

claim: The motor cortex data consists of spiking activity of 89 neurons recorded during the last second of inter-trial-intervals, taken from 600 consecutive trials in one recording session.
source: The data used in this paper, consists of spiking activity of 89 neurons recorded during the last second of inter-trial-intervals, taken from 600 consecutive trials in one recording session.
evidence: This describes the motor cortex dataset used in the analysis.

claim: The auditory cortex recordings consist of 125 experimental sessions recorded from 39 neurons.
source: The data consists of 125 experimental sessions recorded from 39 neurons.
evidence: This describes the auditory cortex dataset from Hershenhoren et al., 2014.

claim: In the basal ganglia recordings from Ito and Doya (2009), 148 NAc and 66 VP neurons across 52 sessions were used for analyses.
source: In total, 148 NAc and 66 VP neurons across 52 sessions were used for analyses (In 18 of the 70 behavioral sessions there were no neural recordings).
evidence: This describes the basal ganglia dataset used in the reanalysis.

claim: A sequence of spike-counts was excluded due to low firing rate if the mean spike count in all blocks was smaller than 1.
source: Following standard procedures (Samejima et al., 2005), a sequence of spike-counts, either simulated or experimentally measured was excluded due to low firing rate if the mean spike count in all blocks was smaller than 1.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria used in the analysis.

claim: This exclusion procedure excluded 0.02% of random-walk neurons and 0.03% of covariance-based plasticity neurons.
source: This procedure excluded 0.02% (4/20,000) of the random-walk neurons and 0.03% (285/1,000,000) of the covariance-based plasticity neurons.
evidence: This reports the results of applying the exclusion criteria to simulated neurons.

claim: 23% of auditory cortex neural recordings were excluded in all 40 randomly assigned sessions.
source: Considering the auditory cortex recordings, we assigned each of the 125 spike counts to 40 randomly-selected sessions. 23% of the neural recordings (29/125) were excluded in all 40 sessions.
evidence: This reports the results of applying exclusion criteria to auditory cortex data.

claim: 11% of basal ganglia recordings were excluded in all 40 randomly-selected sessions.
source: Similarly, considering the basal ganglia neurons, we assigned each of the 642 recordings (214 × 3 phases) to 40 randomly-selected sessions. 11% (74/(214 × 3)) of the recordings were excluded in all 40 sessions.
evidence: This reports the results of applying exclusion criteria to basal ganglia data.

claim: None of the simulated action-value neurons or motor cortex neurons were excluded.
source: None of the simulated action-value neurons (0/20,000) or the motor cortex neurons (0/89) were excluded.
evidence: This reports that no exclusions were necessary for these datasets.
